clips.send: Cold front. Cold air plows under warm air. A fast-moving cold air mass pushes under the warm air and shoves it up steeply. Steep, fast lifting builds tall cumulonimbus clouds: heavy rain, thunderstorms, gusty winds, sometimes hail or tornadoes, but only for a short time. After it passes: temperature drops, pressure rises, the wind shifts (often to the northwest) and skies clear. Map symbol: a blue line with triangles pointing the way it moves.

clips.send: Warm ocean water. The hurricane’s fuel. Hurricanes need ocean water of at least about 26.5 degrees Celsius . Warm water evaporates, loading the air with water vapor. When that vapor condenses into clouds, it releases huge amounts of heat energy. Over land or cold water the fuel is cut off and the storm weakens. Try the ocean-temperature slider!

clips.send: Cumulonimbus. Thunderstorm cloud. A giant tower cloud that can reach 12 km or higher, with a flat anvil top where it hits the stratosphere. Strong updrafts of warm, moist air feed it. It brings lightning, thunder, downpours, hail and sometimes tornadoes. “Cumulus” means heap, and “nimbus” means rain cloud.

clips.send: Spiraling winds. In at the bottom, up, out at the top. Near the ocean surface, air rushes in toward the very low pressure at the center. Earth’s rotation (the Coriolis effect) turns it into a spin: counterclockwise in the Northern Hemisphere, clockwise in the Southern. The air rises in the eyewall and spreads out at the top of the storm. The same kind of storm is called a hurricane (Atlantic), typhoon (western Pacific) or cyclone (Indian Ocean).

clips.send: An air mass is a huge body of air with about the same temperature and humidity throughout, sometimes covering millions of square kilometers. It takes on the character of where it forms: over land it is dry (continental), over ocean it is humid (maritime); near the poles it is cold (polar), near the tropics it is warm (tropical).

clips.send: Warm front. Warm air slides up over cool air. Advancing warm air slowly rises over the cooler air on a gentle slope that can stretch hundreds of kilometers. Clouds arrive in order: high cirrus first (a day or more ahead), then lower, thicker stratus and nimbostratus. It brings long periods of light, steady rain or drizzle. Afterward it is warmer and more humid. Map symbol: a red line with half-circles pointing the way it moves.

clips.send: 低气压，L。空气上升，多云和风暴。低气压中心的空气上升。上升的空气冷却，水汽凝结形成云和降水。地面风向低压中心旋转着吹入，在北半球呈逆时针方向。锋面通常从低压中心向外延伸。气压计读数下降，预示低气压正在靠近。
clips.text: 低气压（L）. 空气上升 → 多云和风暴. 低气压中心的空气上升。上升的空气冷却，水汽凝结形成云和降水。. 地面风向低压中心旋转着吹入，在北半球呈逆时针方向。. 锋面通常从低压中心向外延伸。气压计读数下降，预示低气压正在靠近。

clips.send: 气团是一大团温度和湿度都差不多的空气，可以覆盖几百万平方千米。它的性质取决于它在哪里形成：在陆地上形成就干燥（大陆性），在海洋上形成就潮湿（海洋性）；在高纬度形成就寒冷（极地），在低纬度形成就温暖（热带）。

clips.send: 冷锋。冷空气铲到暖空气下面。快速移动的冷气团插到暖空气下面，把暖空气陡峭地向上推。陡峭而快速的抬升形成高大的积雨云：大雨、雷暴、阵风，有时还有冰雹或龙卷风，但持续时间短。冷锋过境后：气温下降，气压升高，风向转变（常转为西北风），天空转晴。天气图符号：蓝色线条加三角形，三角形指向锋面移动方向。

clips.send: 真实的样子早期气象雷达屏幕上的飓风“艾比”，1960 年它正逼近英属洪都拉斯（今伯利兹）海岸。雷达“看”到的是雨：围着黑色风眼的亮环就是眼墙，螺旋雨带向外弯曲伸展。 · 1960 年图片：NOAA National Weather Service · Public domain · 来源
